screens.title: Smart Contract Interaction Patterns
screens.subtitle: How DApps read state, send transactions, and listen for events

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn the concrete patterns a frontend uses to talk with a deployed smart contract. We focus on the two essential pieces: the contract address, which locates the contract on a network, and the ABI, which describes its public functions and events so your code can call them. You will see how to instantiate an ethers. Contract with just a provider for read-only calls, and with a signer when you need to send transactions that change state. We will walk through calling view and pure functions for free reads, executing state-changing functions that require the user's signature and gas, and subscribing to emitted events so your UI can react in real time. Along the way you'll review common mistakes such as using the wrong ABI, forgetting await, or instantiating a contract without a signer when you mean to send a transaction. By the end, you will be able to wire up a simple Counter contract from compile to frontend integration, deploy locally with Hardhat, and implement event-driven UI updates. Consider how these patterns make a DApp feel responsive while keeping blockchain costs and latency in mind.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A DApp needs the contract address and ABI to instantiate an ethers.Contract; use a provider for reads, a signer for transactions, and events for efficient real-time updates.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to reliably connect a DApp frontend to a deployed smart contract, interpret and use an ABI, call read-only functions without cost, and send signed transactions to modify contract state. First, you'll learn why the contract address and ABI are both required: the address locates the contract on a specific network, while the ABI tells your code which functions and events exist and how to encode parameters. Second, you'll practice calling view and pure functions that return state without creating transactions, which is fast and free. Third, you'll send transactions to payable or state-changing functions; you'll see the wallet prompt, transaction hash, and how to wait for confirmations. Finally, you'll subscribe to events using contract. on to receive push-based updates, a pattern that avoids inefficient polling. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can test your implementation against the provided Hardhat scripts.

screens.title: Contract Address and ABI explained
screens.subtitle: Locate the contract and know its interface

narration.text: Two artifacts are non-negotiable when your frontend wants to interact with a deployed smart contract: the contract address and the ABI. The address is a unique on-chain identifier. It tells your DApp where the contract lives on a specific network such as a local Hardhat node or Sepolia. The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is a JSON description of all public functions and events. It describes each function's name, parameter types, return types, and whether a function is view, pure, or state-changing. Without the correct ABI the frontend cannot encode function calls or decode returned values, which usually results in immediate call errors. A concrete example: after compiling Counter. sol you will find an artifacts JSON that includes the ABI array. Use that exact ABI to construct new ethers. Contract(address, abi, providerOrSigner). A common mistake is to copy a trimmed or hand-rewritten ABI that omits event definitions or changes signatures; that causes mismatches. Key takeaway: always use the artifact ABI that matches the deployed bytecode and ensure the address is for the same network you are connected to. This prevents the most frequent integration errors.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Address locates the contract; ABI describes how to call it. Both must match the deployed instance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Contract Address & ABI
What is a Contract Address?
A contract address is the blockchain location where the contract code and storage live. It is network-specific: an address on a local Hardhat node is different from Sepolia or mainnet.
What is an ABI?
The ABI is a JSON array describing functions and events. It allows libraries like ethers.js to encode function calls and decode return values and event logs.
Key Takeaway

Always use the compiled artifact ABI and deploy address from the same build and network to avoid mismatches.

Concrete Example
After compiling Counter.sol, open artifacts/contracts/Counter.sol/Counter.json and copy the abi array into app.js or import the JSON. Use the address printed by your deploy script as the contract address.
Common Mistake
  • Using an ABI that doesn't match the deployed bytecode.
  • Using an address from a different network than the provider you are connected to.
Mnemonic
Think: address = map location, ABI = dictionary of allowed actions.

screens.title: Instantiating ethers.Contract
screens.subtitle: Provider vs Signer determines read/write capabilities

narration.text: Instantiating a contract is the first practical step to interact with on-chain code. The important choice is whether you pass a provider or a signer when you create the ethers. Contract instance. A provider lets you make read-only calls to view and pure functions; these RPC calls are free and do not require wallet signatures. When you need to send transactions that change state, instantiate the contract with a signer so the library can prompt the user to sign and broadcast a transaction. In code, you will see two common patterns: new ethers. Contract(address, abi, provider) for reads and new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signer) for writes. A common integration mistake is creating the contract once with a provider and later attempting to call state-changing functions without swapping to a signer; this causes a failure at send time. Another pitfall is forgetting to await asynchronous calls, which leads to unresolved promises. In the Counter example you will load the contract once the user connects their wallet, instantiate it with signer, enable the UI controls, and then call getCount or increment depending on the button action. Keep provider usage for UI data fetches and signer when you expect MetaMask to pop up.

keyIdea.title: Practical pattern
keyIdea.text: Use provider for read-only calls and signer for transactions; instantiate accordingly to avoid permission errors.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Instantiating ethers.Contract
Code Walkthrough
This snippet shows the two instantiation patterns used in the chapter. Use the provider-only form for reads and the signer form for sending transactions.
// provider for read-only
const counterWithProvider = new ethers.Contract(counterContractAddress, counterContractABI, provider);

// signer for state-changing functions
const counterWithSigner = new ethers.Contract(counterContractAddress, counterContractABI, signer);
After a user connects a wallet, create the signer from the provider and recreate the contract with that signer so UI controls for transactions become available.
Supporting Notes
  • Provider-only contract cannot send transactions.
  • Signer attaches the user's account for sending and signing transactions.
  • Recreate the contract after the user connects a wallet to avoid permission errors.
Example UI Flow
Disable transaction buttons until you have a signer. Once the contract is instantiated with a signer, enable increment and decrement actions.

screens.title: Calling view/pure vs state-changing functions
screens.subtitle: When to read and when to create a transaction

narration.text: Understanding the difference between read-only calls and transactions is essential for correct DApp behavior and cost control. View and pure functions in Solidity do not modify contract storage. Calling them from a frontend results in an RPC node executing the function locally and returning data; there is no gas cost and no wallet signature is required. For example, getCount in the Counter contract returns the current count as a quick RPC call. By contrast, state-changing functions like increment and decrement modify storage and therefore require a signed transaction. When you call counterContract. increment() with a signer, the user's wallet will present a confirmation, you obtain a transaction hash, and you must wait for the transaction to be mined. This pattern has latency and gas cost implications. A common misconception is that a function labeled non-payable does not cost gas — any state change costs gas. Another frequent error is forgetting await on calls such as tx. wait(), which leads to UI race conditions and stale displays. Concrete example: call getCount() to fetch a number instantly, then when you call increment(), show a pending indicator, wait for tx. wait(), and then re-fetch getCount to update the UI. This sequence keeps the UI consistent and avoids double-counting or stale reads.

keyIdea.title: Compare
keyIdea.text: View/pure are free reads via provider; state-changing functions require signer, gas, and confirmation delays.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › View vs Transaction
Read-only (view / pure)
No wallet signature, no gas. Use provider and call functions like getCount(). Fast and suitable for rendering UI state.
Example
const currentCount = await counterContract.getCount(); // RPC call through provider
State-changing (transactions)
Requires signer and gas. Triggers wallet confirmation and produces a transaction hash. Use tx.wait() to await mining before trusting on-chain state changes.
Example
const tx = await counterContract.increment(); await tx.wait(); // confirm mined
Misconception
Non-payable does not imply free; changing state always consumes gas.
Pro tip
Show a pending state after sending tx and before awaiting confirmation to avoid duplicate submissions.
Check
Always await tx.wait() before re-reading the contract if you need guaranteed final state.

screens.title: Transaction lifecycle in a DApp
screens.subtitle: From user signature to confirmed state

narration.text: Understanding the transaction lifecycle helps you design robust UI flows. The lifecycle begins when the user initiates an action that requires a state change. The frontend sends a transaction request via a signer; the user's wallet displays a confirmation prompt where they review and sign the transaction. Once signed, the library returns a transaction object with a hash indicating the transaction was broadcast. Your app should present that hash and an intermediate pending state. The next step is mining: await tx. wait() to pause until the transaction reaches the configured number of confirmations. Only after confirmation should the UI assume the on-chain state has changed. Errors can occur at any stage: the user may reject the signature, the transaction may revert due to a require condition, or the network may fail to include the transaction. A concrete Counter example: when decrementing, a require prevents the count from going below zero; a revert will be captured by ethers. js and often exposes a revert message in error. data. message. Misconception to avoid: treating broadcast as final — a broadcasted transaction can still fail during mining. Practical pattern: show pending, await confirmation, then refresh your view with a view call or rely on an event listener to update state.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: User signs → tx broadcast (hash) → pending → mined/confirmed (await tx.wait()) → update UI or react to events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Transaction Lifecycle
Transaction Lifecycle
1. User Initiates
Click triggers contract call
2. Wallet Prompt
User signs with MetaMask
3. Broadcast
tx.hash returned
4. Confirm & Finalize
await tx.wait()
Example Flow
User clicks Increment → wallet opens → after signing the app shows transaction hash → await tx.wait() → refresh getCount() or wait for event.
Common Mistakes
  • Treating broadcast as confirmed.
  • Not handling user rejection errors (code 4001).
  • Not extracting revert messages from error.data.message.

screens.title: Listening for Events
screens.subtitle: Use events for push-based UI updates

narration.text: Events are a primary mechanism for frontends to learn about on-chain state changes efficiently. When a contract emits an event, it is recorded in the transaction logs. Libraries like ethers. js expose contract. on(eventName, callback) to subscribe to these emitted events so your DApp can react as soon as the event is mined. For the Counter contract, CountIncremented and CountDecremented include the user address and the new count; when these events fire, the frontend can update the display immediately and show a concise notification. A concrete advantage of event listening is reduced load and latency compared to polling: instead of repeatedly calling getCount, the frontend receives a push notification from the node when a relevant transaction occurs. Important operational notes: remove previous listeners with contract. off to avoid duplicate callbacks if you recreate the contract multiple times, and be careful to subscribe only after the contract is instantiated. A common misconception is that events are emitted before confirmation — they are part of the transaction log, and the frontend should consider the event final once the transaction is mined. Use filters if you want to subscribe to a subset of events or query historical events via queryFilter for a block range.

keyIdea.title: Event-driven
keyIdea.text: Subscribe with contract.on to receive push notifications on events and avoid polling; remove listeners to prevent duplicates.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Listening for Events
Event Listener Pattern
Use contract.off to remove prior listeners, then contract.on to subscribe. The callback receives event args and a full event object, including the transaction hash.
// Example listener counterContract.off("CountIncremented"); counterContract.on("CountIncremented", (user, newCount, event) => { // update UI using newCount });
Why events matter
  • Push-based updates are more efficient than polling.
  • Events include indexed fields to filter important data like user addresses.
  • Historical events can be queried via queryFilter for a block range.
Common Mistake
Attaching listeners multiple times without removing them leads to duplicate UI updates and memory leaks.

screens.title: Counter Contract: Key excerpts
screens.subtitle: Use the contract code to map UI behavior to on-chain logic

narration.text: Reading the contract source helps you design the frontend calls. The Counter contract exposes a public count variable, increment and decrement functions, and events CountIncremented and CountDecremented. Because count is public, Solidity generates a getter that behaves like a view function. Increment simply increments and emits an event; decrement includes a require ensuring the count does not go below zero, and then emits an event. From the frontend perspective, you will call getCount to display the current value. When calling increment or decrement, you must handle the possibility of a revert; decrement will revert if count is zero, and the error may include the revert message. Observing the events allows you to update the UI as soon as transactions are mined. The code excerpt below is from the chapter's source. Study it so you can map each UI control to a contract function and anticipate what parameters and return values to handle. Counter Contract: Key excerpts means counter exposes getcount (view), increment/decrement (state-changing) and emits events used to update the ui in real time.. In practical terms, use the contract code to map ui behavior to on-chain logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract excerpt
keyIdea.text: Counter exposes getCount (view), increment/decrement (state-changing) and emits events used to update the UI in real time.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Counter Contract Excerpts
Solidity Excerpt
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    uint public count;

    event CountIncremented(address indexed user, uint newCount);
    event CountDecremented(address indexed user, uint newCount);

    constructor() { count = 0; }

    function increment() public {
        count++;
        emit CountIncremented(msg.sender, count);
    }

    function decrement() public {
        require(count > 0, "Count cannot go below zero");
        count--;
        emit CountDecremented(msg.sender, count);
    }

    function getCount() public view returns (uint) {
        return count;
    }
}
Map
getCount → frontend read; increment/decrement → signed txs; events → UI updates.
Error case
decrement uses require so it will revert if count is zero — handle this in the UI.
Event use
Events include the user address and newCount to show precise UI changes.

screens.title: Deploy and interact scripts (Hardhat)
screens.subtitle: Run the deploy and interact flow locally to validate behavior

narration.text: A practical way to validate frontend interactions is to deploy Counter to a local Hardhat node and run scripted interactions. The chapter offers a deploy script that compiles and deploys the contract then prints the deployed address. Using that address in an interact script, you can instantiate the contract with a signer on the local provider and reproduce the same sequence your frontend will perform: read initial count, send increment and decrement transactions, and query events with queryFilter. Running npx hardhat node provides a local chain you control; run the deploy script against that node to get a reliable address. The interact script then logs transaction hashes and confirmation messages in your terminal, giving you a deterministic way to trace failure modes, gas behavior, and event logs. This lab approach helps you isolate frontend issues: if the scripts succeed but your app fails, the problem is likely in your frontend wiring, provider selection, or ABI mismatch. Use the example scripts in the chapter exactly, copy the artifact ABI, and replace the placeholder address with the freshly deployed address before running interact. js.

keyIdea.title: Lab pattern
keyIdea.text: Deploy locally with Hardhat, then run scripted interactions to validate contract ABI, address, events, and state changes before wiring the UI.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Deploy & Interact Scripts
Terminal-first Lab
Start a local Hardhat node, run the deploy script to get the address, paste it into interact.js, and run the interaction script to observe state changes and logged events in the terminal.

npx hardhat node

Diagnostic Tip

screens.title: Error handling and revert messages
screens.subtitle: Diagnose require/revert reasons and user rejections

narration.text: Robust DApps handle errors at three places: user rejection, transaction revert, and RPC failures. When a user rejects the wallet prompt, ethers. js commonly surfaces an error with code 4001; handle this case so the UI can inform the user gracefully. When a transaction reverts due to a require or other on-chain check, ethers. js often includes the revert message in error. data. message. For example, calling decrement when count is zero will revert with "Count cannot go below zero". Capture that message and show it to the user rather than a generic failure. RPC failures or network mismatches often manifest as call errors when the contract address or ABI is wrong or when the frontend is connected to the wrong network. Avoid the mistake of swallowing errors: log them in development and surface a concise, actionable message to users in production. Another common mistake is not awaiting async operations; forgetting await before tx. wait leads to unresolved promises and outdated UI state. Concrete pattern: wrap calls in try/catch, inspect error. code and error. data. message when present, and provide distinct UI paths for rejection, revert, and network issues.

keyIdea.title: Errors
keyIdea.text: Differentiate user rejection (code 4001), revert messages (error.data.message), and RPC/network failures; handle each with clear UI feedback.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Error Handling
Diagnose and Surface Errors
Use try/catch around async calls to classify errors and provide helpful messages to users. Distinguish three common cases and respond accordingly.
User rejected
Handle error.code === 4001 and show that the action was cancelled.
Transaction revert
Inspect error.data.message to extract require/revert reason and show it to the user.
Network/RPC
Check address, ABI, and provider network; provide retry or check-network guidance.
Pro Tip

Log full error objects in development, but present concise, actionable messages in production UIs.

screens.title: UI patterns for contract interaction
screens.subtitle: Enable/disable controls, show pending states, and refresh safely

narration.text: A good UI makes clear which actions are allowed and shows clear feedback through the transaction lifecycle. Start by disabling contract controls until the contract is loaded and a signer is available. The chapter demonstrates updateContractUI that toggles button disabled states based on contract load. When sending a transaction, present a pending indicator and optionally the transaction hash so advanced users can inspect it. After tx. wait() confirms the transaction, refresh the displayed state by calling a view function or relying on an event listener to supply the new value. Avoid naive polling: prefer event subscriptions for real-time updates. When you recreate or reload the contract instance, remove existing event listeners with contract. off to prevent duplicate handling. Also, handle edge cases like network changes by clearing listeners and re-initializing the contract on the new provider. Concrete pattern: load contract → enable buttons → on click send tx → show pending → await confirmation → refresh count via getCount() or via event callback. This yields a responsive and safe user experience. UI patterns for contract interaction means disable controls until contract and signer are ready, show pending state during tx, then refresh state via view call or event listener.. In practical terms, enable/disable controls, show pending states, and refresh safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UI pattern
keyIdea.text: Disable controls until contract and signer are ready, show pending state during tx, then refresh state via view call or event listener.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › UI Patterns
Practical UI Patterns
Load State
Disable transaction actions until contract is loaded and signer is present. Use a clear loading indicator so users know why controls are disabled.
Pending & Confirmed
Show pending state after tx is broadcast, and only update the main view after tx.wait or when an event arrives confirming the change.
Event vs Poll
Prefer events for push updates; use polling only for occasional checks or fallback paths.
Listeners
Call contract.off before contract.on when reinitializing to avoid duplicate callbacks.
Network Changes
On network switch, recreate provider, signer, and contract instances and reattach listeners safely.

screens.title: Frontend interaction example (app.js)
screens.subtitle: Load contract, call getCount, send transactions, and listen for events

narration.text: Using the Counter example, the chapter provides a practical app. js sequence that ties everything together. First, ensure a user wallet is connected and derive signer and provider. Store the contract address and a simplified ABI (or import the artifact ABI). Provide UI controls for 'Load Contract', 'Get Current Count', 'Increment', and 'Decrement' and keep them disabled until the contract is loaded. When loading the contract with a signer, recreate the ethers. Contract instance and set up event listeners for CountIncremented and CountDecremented. For read-only actions, call getCount and convert returned BigNumber to a string for display. For state changes, call increment or decrement and show a pending message, then await tx. wait() before trusting the new state. The code in the chapter also demonstrates catching errors, checking error. code for user rejection, and reading error. data. message for revert reasons. This end-to-end wiring — connect wallet, instantiate contract with signer, set up listeners, call view and transaction functions — is the exact flow you'll implement in a real DApp. Frontend interaction example (app.js) means connect wallet → instantiate contract with signer → set listeners → call view for reads and send transactions for state changes.. In practical terms, load contract, call getcount, send transactions, and listen for events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: App flow
keyIdea.text: Connect wallet → instantiate contract with signer → set listeners → call view for reads and send transactions for state changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › app.js Integration
Integration Snippet
// instantiate after wallet connect
counterContract = new ethers.Contract(counterContractAddress, counterContractABI, signer);

// read-only example
const currentCount = await counterContract.getCount();
console.log('Current Count:', currentCount.toString());

// state-changing example
const tx = await counterContract.increment();
console.log('Transaction sent:', tx.hash);
await tx.wait();
console.log('Transaction confirmed');

// event listener
counterContract.off('CountIncremented');
counterContract.on('CountIncremented', (user, newCount, event) => {
  console.log('EVENT: Count Incremented by', user, 'to', newCount.toString());
});
Example Note
Convert returned BigNumber values to string before displaying. Recreate the contract when signer becomes available.
Misconception
Do not assume contract.on fires before confirmation; rely on mined events or tx.wait confirmation for final state.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Hands-on Activity

  2. Run npx hardhat node and deploy with scripts/deploy.js to get address.
  3. Paste the address into scripts/interact.js and run it to observe logs.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, you always need the contract address and a matching ABI to interact with a deployed contract. Second, a provider enables read-only calls to view and pure functions with no gas cost; a signer is required for transactions that modify state. Third, state changes produce transactions: prompt the wallet, provide transaction feedback, and await confirmations. Fourth, events are the efficient, push-based mechanism to update your UI in real time; prefer contract. on over polling whenever possible. These concepts form the backbone of frontend smart contract integration and will let you build responsive and correct DApps. Keep these rules in mind when you connect your app to local Hardhat instances and when you later migrate to testnets or mainnet.
